Calling a callback doesn't stop the function. If you call `callback(err)` in an `if` and forget to return, the code below it runs too, and the callback often gets called a second time.

The rule reports a call to `callback`, `cb` or `next` inside a function, unless the call is returned, is followed by a `return` that ends its block, or is the function's last statement.

ESLint has deprecated this rule. Use `n/callback-return` instead.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
function load(path, callback) {
  readFile(path, (err, text) => {
    if (err) {
      callback(err);
    }
    callback(null, JSON.parse(text));
  });
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
function load(path, callback) {
  readFile(path, (err, text) => {
    if (err) {
      return callback(err);
    }
    callback(null, JSON.parse(text));
  });
}

function check(request, response, next) {
  if (!request.user) {
    next(new Error("Not signed in"));
    return;
  }
  next();
}
```

## Options

The only option is the list of names that count as callbacks. It replaces the default, `["callback", "cb", "next"]`. A name can be a path such as `"response.send"`.

{/* bad {"options": [["done", "response.send"]]} */}
```js
function handle(request, response) {
  if (!request.user) {
    response.send(401);
  }
  response.send(200);
}
```

With the same list, `callback` isn't checked anymore:

{/* good {"options": [["done", "response.send"]]} */}
```js
function load(err, callback) {
  if (err) {
    callback(err);
  }
  finish();
}
```

## When not to use it

The rule only looks at the name, so it can't tell a callback from any other function called `next`. You don't need it in code that uses promises and `async` functions.
